items.title: Phil Woods — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: we heard our first Charlie Parker records, and uh, that’s all she wrote... I knew when I heard Bird that there was some stuff happening... I got thoroughly hooked on music... I knew that Bird was, this was the new music

ctx.x: Well, uh could you talk about your parents?

My parents. Well, my dad was reported to be a violin player when he was a kid. Um, music was very important in our family. My mom loved music. Uh [mumbles] there were four or five sisters and on my father’s side there was an uncle who played saxophone and one of my mother’s sister’s husbands played saxophone and that’s how I, I was given the sax in the will when he died. So music was um an

integral part of our life in those days, because music of course in those days was everybody was dancing to the same beat. I mean we all knew who Irving Berlin was. I remember rides with my mom and dad. They loved the movies. Uh, when we’d go away on vacations and stuff we would sing songs, you know, we knew, we knew the, the score to The Wizard of Oz and uh you know Over the Rainbow and Blue Skies and what have you, you know?. So it wasn’t, it wasn’t like, like music has become where you’ve got the youngest kid…

items.title: Phil Woods interviewed by Monk Rowe, Delaware Water Gap, PA, November 8, 1999
items.q: But at night I would study bebop, Charlie Parker, I’d have the radio on and listen to broadcasts from Birdland

ctx.x: A couple of weeks ago when we had a brief conversation on the phone you said you were taking time these days to do some writing and kind of reflecting. What do you reflect and write on these days?

How lucky I am to make a living doing something I love to do; having a wonderful, supportive family; living in a wonderful part of the world where a lot of young people know who Charlie Parker was and John Coltrane. Delaware Water Gap, you might not be aware of it, but this venerable institution we’re sitting in right now, The Deer Head Inn, has had jazz for over 50 years. Chris and Dona Solliday, they run a three night — at least three nights a week — Friday and Saturday and they usually have a matinee type…
Do you feel jazz is healthier today than it has been in the past?
